bio.en: Michael Truell is the co-founder and CEO of Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, the AI code editor that reached $100M ARR in about a year and a half.
bio.zh: 迈克尔·特鲁埃尔（Michael Truell）是 Anysphere 的联合创始人兼 CEO，该公司打造了 AI 代码编辑器 Cursor，约在一年半内达到 1 亿美元 ARR。

summary.en: Michael describes Cursor's goal of inventing a new way to build software where engineers become "logic designers" specifying intent. He shares the counterintuitive finding that custom models power every magic moment, and that they initially hired too slowly. The episode is a candid founder's view of building the fastest-growing AI developer tool.
summary.zh: 迈克尔描述了 Cursor 的目标：发明一种构建软件的新方式，让工程师变成"逻辑设计者"，只需明确意图。他分享了一个反直觉的发现——每一个魔法时刻背后都有定制模型的支撑，且他们起初招人太慢。本期以坦诚的创始人视角，讲述了如何打造增长最快的 AI 开发者工具。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: ... our goal with Cursor is to invent a new type of programming, a very different way to build software. So a world kind of after code, I think that more and more being an engineer will start to feel like being a logic designer, and really, it will be about specifying your intent for how exactly you want everything to work.
turns.zh: ……我们开发Cursor的目标是开创一种全新的编程范式，一种截然不同的软件构建方式。换句话说，就是在代码之外的世界里，我认为越来越多的工程师将逐渐转变为逻辑设计师，真正专注于明确自己希望一切如何运作的意图。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the most counter-intuitive thing you've learned so far about building Cursor?
turns.zh: 到目前为止，在开发Cursor的过程中，你学到的最违背直觉的事情是什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: We definitely didn't expect to be doing any of our own model development. And at this point, every magic moment in Cursor involves a custom model in some way.
turns.zh: 我们绝对没有预料到需要自己开发模型。在现阶段，Cursor的每一个突破性进展都离不开某种自定义模型的支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something that you wish you knew before you got into this role?
turns.zh: 如果你在入职前就知道以下这些事，会不会更好？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Many people you hear hire too fast, I think we actually hired too slow to begin with.
turns.zh: 我听说很多人招人太快了，但我觉得我们一开始招人速度反而太慢了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You guys went from $0 to 100 million ARR in a year and a half, which is historic. Was there an inflection point where things just started to really take off?
turns.zh: 你们在一年半内就从0做到1亿美元的年化经常性收入，这堪称传奇。是否有某个转折点让业务真正起飞了？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: The growth has been fairly just consistent on an exponential. And exponential to begin with feels fairly slow when the numbers are really low, and it didn't really show off to the races to begin with.
turns.zh: 增长一直相当稳定地呈指数级增长。然而在数字很低的时候，指数增长的速度会显得很慢，起初也并没有明显的爆发式增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think is the secret to your success?
turns.zh: 你认为你们成功的秘诀是什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think it's been...
turns.zh: 我认为……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When we were chatting earlier, you had this really interesting phrase, this idea of what comes after code. Talk about that, just the vision you have of where you think things are going in terms of moving from code to maybe something else.
turns.zh: 之前我们聊天时，你提到了一个很有趣的概念——代码之后会发生什么。能否谈谈你的看法？你对从代码到其他领域的演进路径有何设想？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Our goal with Cursor is to invent sort of a new type of programming, a very different way to build software, that's kind of just distilled down into you describing the intent to the computer for what you want in the most concise way possible, and really distilled down to just defining how you think the software should work, and how you think it should look. With the technology that we have today, and as it matures, we think you can get to a place where you can invent a new method of building software that's [inaudible 00:05:16] higher level, and more productive, in some cases, more accessible too. (00:05:21): And that process will be a gradual moving away from what building software looks like today. I want to contrast it with maybe the vision of what software looks like in the future that I think... A couple of visions that are in a popular consciousness that we at least have some disagreement with. One is, there's a group of people who think that software building in the future is going to look very much like it does today, which mostly means text editing, formal programming languages, like TypeScript, and Go, and C, and Rust. And then there's another group that kind of thinks you're just going to type into a bot, and you're going to ask it to build you something, and then you're going to ask it to change something about what you're building, and it's kind of like this chatbot, Slackbot style where you're talking to your engineering department. (00:06:10): And we think that there are problems with both of those visions. I think that on the chatbot style end of things... And we think it's going to look weirder than both. The problem with the chatbot style end of things is that lacks a lot of precision. If you want humans to have complete control over what the software looks like, and how it works, you need to let them gesture at what they want to be changed in a form factor that's more precise than just, "Change this about my app." In a text box, removed from the whole thing. And then the version of the world where nothing changes we think is wrong, because we think the technology is going to get much, much, much better. (00:06:54): And so a world after code, I think that it looks like a world where you have a representation of the logic of your software that does look more like English, you have written down... You can imagine in [inaudible 00:07:08] form, you can imagine in kind of an evolution of programming language towards pseudocode. You have written down the logic of the software, and you can edit that at a high level, and you can point at that. And it won't be the impenetrable millions of lines of code, it'll instead be something that's much Terser, and easier to understand, easier to navigate. But that world where the kind of crazy, hard to understand symbols start to evolve towards something that's a little bit more human-readable, and human-editable, is one that we're working towards.
turns.zh: 我们开发Cursor的目标是发明一种全新的编程范式，一种截然不同的软件构建方式。核心理念是以最简洁的形式向计算机传达你的需求，重点在于定义软件应有的运行逻辑和视觉呈现。随着技术的成熟，我们相信未来能实现更高层次、更高生产力、更易用的新型软件开发方式。（00:05:21）这种转变将逐步摆脱当今的软件构建模式。我想将其与未来软件可能呈现的两种不同愿景进行对比。第一种观点认为未来的软件构建仍将沿用现有模式——即文本编辑、TypeScript、Go、C、Rust等正式编程语言。这类观点存在局限性；第二种观点则设想用户通过聊天机器人交互式编程，但这种方式缺乏精确性，无法让用户完全掌控软件的逻辑与行为。（00:06:10）我们认为这两种愿景都存在问题。在聊天机器人式编程方面，我们认为其缺乏必要的精确性。若想让用户完全掌控软件的外观与行为，必须以更精准的形式呈现可更改内容，而非在文本框中输入“更改应用某项功能”之类的笼统指令。同时，我们认为现有不变的软件世界是错误的，因为技术将迎来巨大进步。（00:06:54）因此，“代码之后的世界”应呈现出软件逻辑的可视化呈现，类似自然语言的表达。用户可以用伪代码形式记录软件逻辑，进行高层编辑，并进行交互式修改。这种世界将摆脱数百万行难以理解的代码，转而采用更简洁、易于理解和导航的形式。我们正朝着这个方向努力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a profound point. I want to make sure people don't miss what you're saying here, which is that what you're envisioning in the next year essentially is kind of when things start to shift, is, people move away from even seeing code, having to think in code in JavaScript and Python, and there's this abstraction that will appear, essentially pseudocode, describing what the code should be doing more in English sentences.
turns.zh: 这是一个深刻的观点。我们希望确保大家不会忽略你在这里所说的核心观点——即你对未来一年的设想，实质上是当事物开始发生转变之际，人们甚至不再需要直面代码，不必用JavaScript和Python语言进行编程思考，取而代之的是一种抽象化的表达——本质上类似伪代码的描述，用更通顺的英文句子来阐述代码应该实现的功能。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yep. We think it ends up looking like that, and we're very opinionated that that path goes through existing professional engineers, and it looks like this evolution away from code. And it definitely looks like the human still being in the driver's seat, and the human having both a ton of control over all aspects of the software and not giving that up. And then also the human having the ability to make changes very quickly, having a fast duration loop and not just having something in the background that's super slow and takes weeks, go do all your work for you.
turns.zh: 没错。我们认为最终会发展成这样，而且我们坚信这条路径会经过现有专业工程师的历程，经历从代码向抽象的演变。人类始终会掌握主动权，既能全方位把控软件的各个方面，又不会将控制权拱手让人。同时，人类还将具备快速调整的能力，不必在背景进程中等待数周才能完成所有工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This begs the question for people that are currently engineers, or thinking about becoming engineers, or designers, or product manager, what skills do you think will be more and more valuable in this world of what comes after code?
turns.zh: 这就引出了一个问题——对于那些目前身为工程师，或正考虑转行成为工程师、设计师或产品经理的人们，你们认为在后代码时代的世界中，哪些技能将变得愈发重要？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think taste will be increasingly more valuable. And I think often when people think about tastes in the realm of software, they think about visuals, or taste over smooth animations, and coloring things, UI, UX, et cetera on the visual design of things. And the visual side of things is an important part of defining a piece of software, but then, as mentioned before, I think that the other half of defining a piece of software is the logic of it, and how the thing works. (00:09:22): And we have amazing tools for specing out the visuals of things, and then when you get into the logic of how a piece of software works, really, the best representation we have of that is code right now. You can kind of gesture at it with Figma, and you can gesture at it with writing down notes, but it's when you have an actual working prototype. And so I think that more and more, being an engineer will start to feel like being a logic designer, and really, it will be about specifying your intent for how exactly you want everything to work. It'd be more about the whats, and a little bit less about how exactly you're going to do things under the hood. (00:09:59): I think taste will be increasingly important. I think one aspect of software engineering, and we're very far from this right now, and there are lots of funny memes going around the internet about some of the trials and tribulations people can run into if they trust AI for too many things that comes to engineering, around building apps that have glaring deficiencies, and problems, and functionality issues. But I think we will get to a place where you'll be able to be less careful as a software engineer, which, right now, is an incredibly, incredibly important skill. We'll move a little bit from carefulness, and a little bit more towards taste.
turns.zh: 我认为审美能力将变得越来越重要。人们谈及软件领域的审美时，往往会想到视觉效果，或是流畅动画的呈现，以及UI、UX等视觉设计层面的问题。视觉设计固然是定义软件的重要组成部分，但正如前文所言，软件的逻辑架构——即其运作原理——同样至关重要。（00:09:22）目前我们拥有出色的工具来设计软件的视觉效果，但当涉及软件的逻辑运作时，目前最佳的呈现方式依然是代码。你可以用Figma进行示意，或是手写笔记，但只有实际可运行的原型才能真正传达你的设计意图。因此，我认为未来工程师的工作将逐渐转向逻辑设计师的角色，重点在于明确软件的运行逻辑，而非深挖底层实现细节。（00:09:59）我相信审美能力将变得日益重要。目前我们距离这一目标尚有距离，网络上流传着许多因过度依赖AI进行工程开发而导致应用出现严重缺陷的趣图。但我相信未来我们将能够降低工程师的谨慎程度，转而更加注重审美能力的培养。毕竟，当前谨慎求全的思维模式是至关重要的技能。我们将逐渐从过度谨慎转向更注重审美价值的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This makes me think of vibe coding, is that kind of what you're describing when you talk about not having to think about the details as much, and just kind of going with the flow?
turns.zh: 这让我联想到“vibe coding”（随心编程）理念——即无需过多纠结于细节，顺其自然地完成开发？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think it's related. I think that vibe coding right now describes exactly this state of creation that is pretty controversial, where you're generating a lot of coding, you aren't really understanding the details. That is a state of creation that then has lots of problems, you don't really... By not understanding the details under the hood right now, you then very quickly get to a place where you're kind of limited at a certain point, where you create something that's big enough that you can't change. And so I think some of the ideas that we're interested around, how do you give people continued control over all the details when they don't really understand the code? I think that solutions there are very relevant to the people who are vibe coding right now. I think that right now, we lack the ability to let the tastemakers actually have complete control over the software. One of the issues also with vibe coding, and letting taste really shine through from people is, you can create stuff, but a lot of it the AI making decisions that are unwieldy and you don't have to control over.
turns.zh: 我觉得这两者有关联。我认为当下的“Vibe编码”（vibe coding）现象，恰恰描述了一种颇具争议的创作状态——你编写了大量代码，却并不真正理解其中的细节。这种创作状态会带来诸多问题，因为你没有深入理解底层逻辑，最终会陷入某种局限：当你创建的系统规模过大时，就无法进行后续修改了。所以我认为，我们目前关注的核心问题是，如何在人们不完全理解代码的情况下赋予他们对所有细节的持续控制权？我认为这些解决方案与当下热衷于“Vibe编码”的人群息息相关。现阶段，我们缺乏让行业领军人物完全掌控软件的能力。此外，Vibe编码也存在一个问题——人们虽能创造出作品，但其中很多是由AI做出难以控制的决策，用户对此毫无把控权。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One more question along these lines. You threw out this word taste. When you say taste, what are you thinking?
turns.zh: 再提一个相关问题。你提到的“taste”（品味）这个词，具体指什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I'm thinking having the right idea for what should be built. It will become more and more about effortless translation of, here's exactly what you want built, here's how you want everything to work, here's how you want it to look. And then you'll be able to make that on a computer, and it will less be about this kind of translation layer of, you and your team have a picture of what you'd want to build, and then you have to really painstakingly, labor-intensive, lay out that into a format that a computer can then execute and interpret. I think less than the UI side of things, maybe taste is a little bit of a misnomer, but just about having the right idea for what should be built.
turns.zh: 我认为它指的是对产品本质的正确构想。未来将更多地关注无缝转换——准确传达你想构建的内容、功能逻辑和视觉效果，然后在计算机上实现。这将不再是那种你和团队先构思产品，再费力地将其转化为计算机可执行格式的过程。相较于用户界面层面，品味或许是个不太准确的术语，但它本质上指的是对产品本质的清晰构想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. I'm going to come back to these topics, but I want to actually zoom us back out to the beginnings of Cursor. I have never heard the origin story, I don't think many people know how this whole thing started. Basically you guys are building one of the fastest growing products in the history of the world, it's changing the way people build products, it's changing careers, professions, it's changing so much. How did it all begin? Any memorable moments along the journey of the early days?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我会回归这些话题，但首先我想回溯到Cursor的起源。我从未听过它的诞生故事，相信很多人也不了解这个项目是如何起步的。基本上，你们打造了全球发展最快的产品之一，它正在重塑人们的开发方式，改变职业生涯和行业格局。这一切是如何开始的？早期阶段有什么难忘的时刻吗？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Cursor kind of started as a solution search of a problem, and a little bit where it very much came from reflecting on how AI was going to get better over the course of the next 10 years. There were kind of two defining moments, one was being really excited by using the first beta version of Code Pilot, actually. This was the first time we had used an AI product that was really, really, really useful, and was actually just useful at all, and wasn't just a vaporware kind of demo thing. (00:13:43): And in addition to being the first AI product that we'd use that was useful, Code Pilot was also one of the most useful, if not the most useful dev tool we'd ever adopted, and that got us really excited. Another moment that got us really excited was the series of scaling on papers coming out of OpenAI and other places that showed that even if we had no new ideas, AI was going to get better and better just by pulling on simple levers, like scaling up the models, and also scaling up the data that was going into the models. (00:14:12): And so at the end of 2021, beginning of 2022, this got us excited about how AI products were now possible, this technology was going to mature into the future. And it felt like when we looked around, there were lots of people talking about making models, and it felt like people weren't really picking an area of knowledge work and thinking about what it was going to look like as AI got better and better. And that set us on the path to an idea generation exercise, it was like, "How are these areas of knowledge work going to change in the future as this tech gets more mature? What is the end state of the work going to look like? How are the tools that we use to do that work going to change? How are the models going to need to get better to support changes in the work? And once scaling and pre-training ran out, how are you going to keep pushing for technological capabilities?" (00:15:07): And the misstep at the beginning of Cursor is we actually worked on... We sort of did this whole grand exercise, and we decided to work on an area of knowledge work that we thought would be relatively uncompetitive, and sleepy, and boring, and no one would be looking at it, because we thought, "Oh, coding's great, coding's totally going to change with this AI, but people are already doing that." So there was a period of four months to begin with, where we were actually working on a very different idea, which was helping to automate and augment mechanical engineering, and building tools for mechanical engineers. (00:15:44): There were problems from the get-go in that. Me and my co-founders, we weren't mechanical engineers. We had friends who were mechanical engineers, but we were very much unfamiliar with the field. So there was a little bit of a blind man and the elephant problem from the get-go. There were problems around, how would you actually take the models that exist to today and make them useful for mechanical engineering? The way we netted out is, you need to actually develop your own models from the get-go. And the way we did that was tricky, and there's not a lot of data on the internet of 3D models of different tools and parts, and the steps that I expect to build up to those 3D models, and then getting them from the sources that have them is also a tricky process too. (00:16:30): But eventually what happened was, we came to our senses, we realized we're not super excited about mechanical engineering, it's not the thing we want to dedicate our lives to. And we looked around, and in the area of programming, it felt like despite a decent amount of time ensuing, not much has changed, and it felt like the people that were working on the space maybe had a disconnect with us, and it felt like they weren't being sufficiently ambitious about where everything was going to go in the future, and how all of software creation was going to blow through these models. And that's what set us off on the path to building Cursor.
turns.zh:
Cursor最初源于对某个问题的解决方案探索，关键的转折点在于对未来十年AI技术进步的深思熟虑。其中有两个决定性时刻：第一个是我们对Code Pilot的首个测试版感到无比兴奋。这是我们首次使用真正实用的AI产品——它不再是虚无缥缈的演示，而是切实提升生产力的工具。（00:13:43）  

除了Code Pilot是我们用过的最有用的AI工具外，它也是我们采用过的最有用的开发工具之一。这让我们激动不已。另一个激动人心的时刻是OpenAI等机构发布的一系列扩展研究论文，这些研究表明，即便我们没有新创意，AI只需通过提升模型规模和数据量等简单手段就能不断进步。（00:14:12）  

2021年底至2022年初，我们对AI产品的可行性充满期待，这项技术将随着时间成熟。然而当时人们热衷于模型训练，却忽视了AI进步对特定领域工作的深远影响。这促使我们开启创意探索之旅：未来随着技术成熟，哪些知识工作领域将发生变革？最终状态会是什么样？支持这些变革所需的工具和模型又将如何升级？当扩展和预训练技术达到极限后，如何持续推动技术进步？  

Cursor项目初期的失误在于，我们选择了一个竞争激烈、缺乏创新且乏味的机械工程领域，认为编程领域会被AI彻底革新，但现实并非如此。（00:15:07）  

这个四个月的探索之旅困难重重。我们与联合创始人并非机械工程师，虽然有朋友是机械工程师，但我们对该领域完全陌生。项目伊始就面临诸多挑战：如何让现有模型适用于机械工程？最终我们意识到必须从头开发专属模型，但获取3D模型数据和构建步骤的难度超出想象。（00:16:30）  

最终我们清醒过来，意识到对机械工程缺乏热情，这并非我们毕生追求的方向。转而将目光投向编程领域，发现这里同样充满机遇。
尽管过了相当长的时间，但情况几乎没有改善。我们感觉那些负责开发该平台的人似乎与我们存在沟通障碍，他们对未来产品的发展方向缺乏足够的雄心壮志，也没有清晰的规划去突破现有模式的局限。正因如此，我们才踏上了开发Cursor平台的征程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So interesting. Okay, so first of all, I love that... This is advice that you often hear of go after a boring industry because no one's going to be there, and there's opportunity. And sometimes it works, but I love that in this journey, it's like, "No, actually, go after the hottest, most popular space, AI coding, app building." And it worked out. And the way you phrased it just now is, you didn't see enough ambition potentially, that you thought there was more to be done. So it feels like that's an interesting lesson. Even if something looks like, "Okay, it's too late, there's GitHub, Code Pilot's out there." Some other products. If you notice that they're just not as ambitious as they could be, or as you are, or you see almost a flaw in their approach, that there's still a big opportunity. Does that resonate?
turns.zh: 好的，真有意思。首先，我很欣赏你提到的这个观点……通常人们会建议选择那些冷门行业，因为竞争少、机会多。但有时这种策略确实有效。不过在你的创业历程中，你却选择了最热门、最受欢迎的领域——人工智能编程和应用开发——而且还取得了成功。这让我觉得这是一个很有启发的教训。即便面对现成的解决方案，比如GitHub、Code Pilot等产品时，如果你发现它们的野心不足，或者与你的期望有落差，那其实仍蕴藏着巨大的机遇。这点你说得太到位了。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: That totally resonates. A part of it is, you need there to be leapfrogs that can happen, you need there to be things that you can do. And I think the exciting thing about AI is, in a bunch of places, and I think this is very much still true of our space, and can talk about how we think about that and how we deal with that, but I think that just the ceiling is really high. And yes, if you look around, probably even if you take the best tool, any of these fields, there should be a lot more that needs to be done over the next few years. Having that space, having that high ceiling, I think is unique amongst areas of software, at least the degree to which it is high with AI.
turns.zh: 我完全赞同你的观点。关键在于，要有跨越式的创新机遇，必须有值得深耕的领域。人工智能领域尤其令人兴奋，在许多细分领域（包括我们所在的领域），这种机遇依然存在。我们可以探讨如何把握机遇、如何应对挑战，但最重要的是，这个领域的上限极高。如果你环顾四周，纵观所有领域，哪怕是用最先进的工具，未来几年仍有大量工作要做。这种广阔的发展空间和极高的上限，在软件领域中实属罕见，至少在人工智能领域，这种上限的设定远超其他领域。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's come back to the IDE questions. So there's a few routes you could have taken, and other companies are doing different routes. So there's building an IDE for engineers to work within and adding AI magic to it, there's another route of just a full AI agentic dev product, and then there's just a model that is very good at coding, and focusing on building the best possible coding model. What made you decide and see that the IDE path was the best route?
turns.zh: 回到IDE开发的问题。其实有多种发展路径，其他公司也在探索不同的方向。比如，为工程师打造集成开发环境（IDE）并注入AI技术；打造全功能的AI编程助手产品；或者专注于开发高性能的编码模型。是什么让你认定IDE路径是最优选择的？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: The folks who were from the get-go working on just a model were working on end-to-end automation programming. I think they were trying to build something very different from us, which is, we care about giving humans control over all of the decisions in the end tool that they're building. And I think those folks were very much thinking of a future where end-to-end, the whole thing is done by AI, and maybe the AI is making all the decisions too. And so, one, there was a personal interest component. Two, I think that always, we've tried to be intense realists about where the technology is today, very, very, very excited about how AI is going to mature over the course of many decades. But I think that sometimes people... There's an instinct to see AI do magical things in one area, and then kind of anthropomorphize these models, and think it's better than a smart person here, and so it must be better than a smart person there. (00:19:55): But these things have massive issues, and we... From the very start, our product development process was really about dogfooding, and using the tool intensely every day. And we never wanted to ship anything that wasn't useful to us, and we had the benefit of doing that because we were the end users part of our product. And I think that that instills a realism in you around where the tech is right now, and so that definitely made us think that we need the humans to be in the driver's seat, the AI cannot do everything. We're also interested in giving humans that control too for personal reasons, and so that gets you away from just your model company that also gets you away from just this end-end stuff without the human having control. (00:20:39): And then the way you get to an IDE versus maybe a plug-in to an existing coding environment is the belief that programming is going to flow through these models, and the active programming is going to change a lot over the course of the next few years. And that the extensibility that existing coding environments have is so, so, so limited, so if you think that the UIs may change a lot, if you think that the form factor programming is going to change a lot, necessarily need to have control over the entire application.
turns.zh: 那些从一开始就专注于模型开发的人，他们致力于端到端自动化编程。我认为他们试图打造与我们截然不同的东西——我们致力于让用户在所构建的最终工具中完全掌控所有决策。而那些人显然设想了一个未来，即未来一切都由AI完成，所有决策也都由AI来做。因此，一方面存在个人兴趣的因素；另一方面，我认为我们始终秉持务实的态度看待当下技术现状。我们对AI未来几十年的发展前景充满期待，但有时人们会因为AI在某个领域展现出的神奇能力，而将这些模型拟人化，将其视为比人类更优秀的存在。（00:19:55）但这些技术存在诸多难题，我们……从一开始，我们的产品开发流程就强调“自用即验证”，每天密集使用工具。我们从不推送对自己无用的功能，而这得益于我们自身就是产品的最终用户。这让我们清醒认识到当前技术的局限性，也促使我们坚信必须让用户掌握主导权——AI无法包办一切。出于个人考量，我们也希望赋予用户自主控制权。这使我们避开了纯模型公司模式，也摆脱了端到端自动化却缺乏用户控制权的困境。（00:20:39）而选择IDE而非现有编程环境插件的核心逻辑在于：我们相信编程将通过这些模型实现深度融合，未来几年主动编程模式将发生巨变。而现有编程环境的扩展性极其有限。若你认为UI会大幅革新，编程范式将彻底变革，就必须掌控整个应用全局。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that you guys today have an IDE, and that's probably the bias you have of this is maybe where the future is heading, but I'm just curious, do you think a big part of the future is also going to be AI engineers that are just sitting in Slack and just doing things for you? Is that something that fits into Cursor one day?
turns.zh: 我知道你们现在有IDE了，这或许是你们对未来的偏见，但我很好奇，你们是否认为未来很大一部分会是AI工程师坐在Slack上为你操盘？这种模式是否能融入Cursor的生态？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think you'll want the ability to move between all of these things fairly effortlessly, and sometimes I think you will want to have the thing kind of go spin off on its own for a while, and then I think you'll want the ability to pull in the AI's work, and then work with it very, very, very quickly, and then maybe have it go spin off again. And so these kind of background versus foreground form factors, I think you want that all to work well in one place. And I think the background stuff, there's a segment of programming that it's especially useful for, which is type of programming tasks where it's very easy to specify exactly what you want without much description, and exactly what correctness looks like without much description. (00:22:05): Bug fixes are a great example of that, but it's definitely not all of programming. So I think that what the IDE is will totally change over time, and our approach to having our own editor was premised on, it's going to have to evolve over time. And I think that that will both include, you can spin off things from different surface areas like Slack, or your issue tracker, or whatever it is, and I think that will also include the pane of glass that you're staring at is going to change a lot. We just mostly think of an IDE as the place where you are building software.
turns.zh: 我认为你会希望能在这些不同的事物之间无缝切换，有时你可能希望某个功能能暂时独立运行一段时间，然后再整合人工智能的成果并快速处理。就背景与前台功能的交互而言，我认为你需要确保所有这些功能在同一平台上能完美协同。特别是对于那些只需精确描述需求且易于验证正确性的编程任务，比如修复漏洞，AI 的辅助作用会非常显著，但这绝非编程的全部应用场景。因此，IDE 的功能将随着时间不断演变。我们最初开发编辑器的初衷就是，它必须随技术发展而更新。我认为这既包括从 Slack、issue tracker 等不同平台抽取信息，也包括彻底重构当前编辑器界面。我们大多将 IDE 视为软件开发的核心平台。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think something people don't talk enough about with talking about agents and all these AI engineers that are going to be doing all this stuff for you, is basically we're all becoming engineering managers, with a lot of reports that are just not that smart, and you have to do a lot of reviewing, and approving, and specifying. I guess thoughts on that, and is there anything you could do to make that easier? Because that sounds really hard. Anyone that has had a large team, being like, "Oh my god, all these junior people just checking in with me doing not high quality work over and over." It's just like, "What a life. It's going to suck."
turns.zh: 在谈论智能助手和那些将为你处理所有事务的 AI 工程师时，人们往往忽略了一点——我们正逐渐成为工程管理者，手下许多员工智力水平有限，需要耗费大量精力进行审查、批准和规范工作。对此你有何看法？有没有什么办法能让这项工作更轻松？因为这听起来实在太难了。任何管理过大型团队的人都会感慨：“天哪，初级员工反复提交低质量代码，真是让人头疼。”这简直是“折磨人的工作”。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe you [inaudible 00:23:12] one-on-ones with [inaudible 00:23:15].
turns.zh: 或许你可以和[00:23:12不可听清]进行一对一交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So many one-on-ones.
turns.zh: 太多一对一交流了。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah. So the customers we've seen have most success with AI I think are still fairly conservative about some of the ways in which they use this stuff. And so I do think today, the most successful customers really lean on things like our next edit prediction, where your coding is normal, and making the next into actions you're going to do. And then they also really lean on scoping down the stuff that you're going to hand off to the bot, and for a fixed percent of your time spent reviewing code, from an agent, or from an AI overall, you could... There's two patterns. One is, you could spend a bunch of time specifying things up front, the AI goes and works, and then you then go and review the AI's work, and then you're done. That's the whole task. (00:24:07): Or you can really chop things up. So you can specify a little bit, AI writes something, review, specify a little bit, AI writes something, review. Autocompletes all in the way of that spectrum. And still we see often the most successful people using these tools are chopping things up right now, and keeping things fairly [inaudible 00:24:28].
turns.zh: 是的。我认为目前在 AI 应用方面最成功的客户，在使用这些技术时仍然相当保守。比如，我们的下一个编辑预测功能：当你的代码正常运行时，它能将下一步操作转化为可执行的任务。此外，他们还会严格控制交给机器人处理的任务范围，并设定固定比例的时间用于审核代码——无论是来自代理还是整体 AI 的代码。可以分为两种模式：一种是前期大量规范需求，AI 执行后再进行审核；另一种是将任务分割成小块，规范一部分，AI 执行一部分，再审核。自动补全功能也处于这个范围之内。不过我们发现，目前最成功的用户往往会将任务分割成小块，并保持较高的代码审查频率。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds less terrible. I'm glad there's a solution here. I want to go back to you guys building Cursor for the first time. What was the point where you realized this is ready? What was a moment of, "Okay, I think this is time to put it out there, and see what happens"?
turns.zh: 听起来情况没那么糟糕了。很高兴这里有解决方案。我想回想一下你们最初开发Cursor的经历。是什么让你们意识到产品已经准备好了？又是什么让你们觉得是时候向公众发布并观察反馈了？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: So when we started building Cursor, we were fairly paranoid about spinning for a while, without releasing to the world. And so to begin with too, we actually... The first version of Cursor was hand-rolled. Now we use VS Code as a base, like many browsers use Chromium as a base, and hit foot off of that. To begin with, we didn't, and built the prototype of Cursor from scratch, and that involved a lot of work. We had to build our own... There were a lot of things that go into a modern code editor, including support for many different languages, and navigation support for moving amongst the language, error tracking support for things. There's things like an integrated command line, the ability to use remote servers, the ability to connect to remote servers to view and run code. And so we kind of just went on this blitz of building things incredibly quickly, building our own editor from scratch, and then also the AI components. (00:25:45): It was after maybe five weeks that we were living on the editor full-time, and had thrown away our previous editor, and we're using a new one. And then once it got to a point where we found it a bit useful, then we put it in other people's hands, and had this very short beta period. And then we launched it out to the world within a couple of months from the first line of code, I think it was probably three months. And it was definitely a, "Let's just get this out to people and build in public quickly." The thing that took us by surprise is we thought we would be building for a couple hundred people for a long time. And from the get-go, there was an immediate rush of interest, and a lot of feedback too. That was super helpful, we learned from that. That's actually why we switched to being based off of VS Code instead of just this hand-rolled thing. A lot of that was motivated by the initial user feedback, and then had been iterating in public from there.
turns.zh: 我们刚开始开发Cursor时，对未向公众发布的担忧特别大。所以最初，我们实际上是从零开始手动编写的。现在我们以VS Code为基础，就像许多浏览器基于Chromium开发一样。最初，我们没有这样做，而是从零开始构建Cursor的原型，这耗费了大量精力。我们必须开发自己的……现代代码编辑器需要包含许多功能，比如支持多种语言、代码导航、错误追踪、集成命令行、远程服务器连接等。在短短几周内，我们就完成了编辑器的开发，彻底抛弃了之前的版本，转而使用新版。等到产品初具规模后，我们立即向外界测试，并在几个月内（大概三个月）就向公众发布了。当时我们的想法就是：“赶紧让产品上线，然后在公开环境中快速迭代。”最令我们惊喜的是，原本以为要花很长时间为几百个用户开发，结果从一开始就吸引了大量关注和反馈。这对我们帮助很大，也是我们转向基于VS Code而非手动编写的原因。很多决策都是基于用户反馈做出的迭代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like how you understated the traction that you got. I think you guys went from $0 to 100 million ARR in a year, year and a half or something like that, which is historic. What do you think was the key to success of something like this? You just talked about dogfooding being a big part of it. You built it in three months, that's insane. What do you think is the secret to your success?
turns.zh: 你把获得的用户反响描述得很低调。我记得你们在一年半左右的时间里，从0做到1亿年化收入，堪称历史级别的成功。你认为成功的关键是什么？你提到内部测试对产品优化很重要。三个月内完成开发，简直不可思议。你觉得成功的秘诀是什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: The three-month version wasn't very good, and so I think it's been a sustained paranoia about, there are all of these ways in which this thing could get better. The end goal is really to invent a very new form of programming that involves automating a lot of coding, as we know today. And no matter where we are with Cursor, it feels like we're very, very far away from that end goal, there's always a lot to do. A lot of it hasn't been over rotated on that initial push, but instead is the continued evolution of the tool, and just making the tool consistently better.
turns.zh: 三个月版本的质量并不理想，所以我们一直保持着持续的警惕，认为产品还有很多可以改进的地方。最终目标是创造一种全新的编程范式，实现当今我们所熟知的编码自动化。无论Cursor目前处于哪个阶段，距离这个终极目标都还很遥远，总有大量工作要做。很多改进并非最初的突破性成果，而是工具的持续进化和不断优化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was there an inflection point after those three months where things just started to really take off?
turns.zh: 三个月后有没有某个转折点，产品开始真正起飞？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: To be honest, it felt fairly slow to begin with, and maybe it comes from some impatience on our part. I think there's the overall speed of the growth which continues to take us by surprise. I think one of the things that has been most surprising too is that the growth has been fairly just consistent on an exponential, of just consistent month-over-month growth, accelerated at times by launches on our part and other things. But an exponential to begin with feels fairly slow and the numbers are really low, and so it didn't really feel off to the races to begin with.
turns.zh: 老实说，一开始进展相当缓慢，这可能源于我们自身的急躁情绪。我认为整体增长速度之快始终令人惊喜。最令人惊讶的是，增长速度相当稳定且呈指数级增长——每月增长率始终如一，有时还会因我们的产品发布等因素而加速。但指数级增长一开始确实感觉很慢，数据量也很低，所以一开始并没有那种势如破竹的感觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To me this sounds like build it and they will come actually working. You guys just built an awesome product that you loved yourselves as engineers, you put it out, people just loved it, told everyone about it.
turns.zh: 在我看来，这听起来像是"只要你搭建好平台，用户自然会来"的典型案例。你们开发了一款自己作为工程师都深爱其产品的出色产品，推向市场后，人们就爱不释口，口口相传。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: It being essentially all just us, the team working on the product, and making the product good in lieu of other things one could spend one's time on. We definitely spent time on tons of other things, for instance, building the team was incredibly important, and doing things like support rotations are very important. But some of the normal things that people would maybe reach for in building the company early on, we really let those fires burn for a long time, especially when it came to things like sales and marketing. (00:29:15): And so just working on the product, and building a product that you like first, your team likes, and then also then adjusting it for some set of users, that can kind of sound simple, but then, as you know, it's hard to do that well. And there are a bunch of different directions one could have run in, a bunch of different product directions. (00:29:35): I think focus, and strategically picking the right things to build, and prioritizing effectively is tricky. I think another thing that's tricky about this domain is, it's kind of a new form of product building, where it's very interdisciplinary in that we are something in between a normal software company and then a foundation model company, in that we're developing a product for millions of people, and that side of things has to be excellent, but then also one important dimension of product quality is doing more and more on the science, and doing more and more on the model side of things in places where it makes sense. And so that element of things doing that well too has been tricky. The overall thing would note is maybe some of these things sound simple to specify, but doing them well is hard, and they're a lot of different way you can run in.
turns.zh: 团队基本上就只有我们这些专注于产品开发的人，其他本可以投入时间的方向都被搁置了。比如，组建团队至关重要，轮流提供支持服务也非常重要。但早期创业公司常做的一些事情，比如销售和市场推广，我们却放任不管了很久。（00:29:15）所以专注于产品开发，先打造一款自己和团队都喜欢的产品，再针对特定用户群体进行调整，这听起来简单，但实际上很难做到。可能有无数种产品方向可选，但关键在于专注，战略性地选择正确的开发方向，并有效分配优先级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to have Andrew Luo joining us today. Andrew is CEO of OneSchema, one of our podcast sponsors. Welcome, Andrew.
turns.zh: 我很高兴今天安德鲁·罗能加入我们。安德鲁是我们的播客赞助商OneSchema的首席执行官。欢迎你，安德鲁。

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny. Great to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请，莱尼。很高兴能来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what is new with OneSchema? I know that you work with some of my favorite companies, like Ramp, and [inaudible 00:30:46], and Watershed. I heard you guys launched a new data intake product that automates the hours of manual work that teams spent importing, and mapping, and integrating CSV in Excel files?
turns.zh: 那么OneSchema有什么新进展吗？我知道你们与我喜欢的几家公司合作，比如Ramp、[00:30:46听不清]和Watershed。我听说你们推出了一个新的数据导入产品，能自动化完成团队在Excel文件中导入、映射和整合CSV数据所耗费的数小时人工操作？

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: Yes. So we just launched the 2.0 of OneSchema FileFeeds. We've rebuilt it from the ground up with AI. We saw so many customers coming to us with teams of data engineers that struggled with the manual work required to clean messy spreadsheets. FileFeeds 2.0 allows non-technical teams to automate the process of transforming CSV and Excel files with just a simple prompt. We support all of the trickiest file integrations, SFTP, S3, and even email.
turns.zh: 是的。我们刚刚推出了OneSchema FileFeeds 2.0版本。我们从头到尾用AI技术进行了全面重建。我们发现许多客户带着数据工程师团队来找我们，他们在清理混乱的电子表格时遇到了繁琐的手动工作。FileFeeds 2.0让非技术团队只需简单提示，就能自动化处理CSV和Excel文件的转换流程。我们支持所有最复杂的文件集成方式，包括SFTP、S3，甚至邮件接收。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to take this off our roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema.
turns.zh: 我可以告诉你，如果我的团队必须开发这样的集成功能，能把这项任务从我们的路线图中移除，转而使用OneSchema这样的工具，那该有多好啊。

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of outages from even just a single bad record, in transactions, employee files, purchase orders, you name it. Debugging these issues is often like finding a needle in a haystack. OneSchema stops any bad data from entering your system, and automatically validates your files, generating error reports with the exact issues in all bad files.
turns.zh: 当然，Lenny。我们听过太多因为单个错误记录导致交易中断、员工档案出错、采购订单失效等问题的可怕案例。排查这些问题往往就像大海捞针。OneSchema能阻止任何错误数据进入你的系统，还能自动验证文件质量，生成错误报告，准确指出所有文件中的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Andrew, thank you so much for joining me. If you want to learn more, head on over to oneschema.co., that's oneschema.co. (00:32:05): What is the most counterintuitive thing you've learned so far about building Cursor, building AI products?
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据会让客户非常头疼，甚至迅速失去信任。Andrew，非常感谢你今天加入我们的对话。如果你想了解更多信息，可以访问oneschema.co。（00:32:05）：在构建Cursor、开发AI产品方面，你遇到过最违反直觉的事情是什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think one thing that's been counterintuitive for us, [inaudible 00:32:14] added a little bit before, but is, we definitely didn't expect to be doing any of our own model development when we started. As mentioned, when we got into this, there were companies that were immediately from the get-go going and just focusing on training model from scratch. And we had done the calculation for what it to train before, and just knew that that was not [inaudible 00:32:36] going to be able to do. And also felt a bit like focusing one's attention in the wrong area, because there were lots of amazing models out there, and why develop all this work to replicate what other players had done. Especially on the pre-training side of things, taking a neural network that knows nothing, and then teaching it the whole internet. (00:32:55): And so we thought we weren't going to be doing that at all, and it seems clear to us from the start that the existing models, there were lots of things that they could be doing for us that they weren't doing, because there wasn't the right tool built for them. In fact though, we do a ton of model development, and internally, it's a big focus for us on the hiring front, and have assembled a fantastic team there. (00:33:18): And it's also been a big win on the product quality side of things for us. And at this point, every magic moment in Cursor involves a custom model in some way. So that was definitely counterintuitive, and surprising, and it's been a gradual thing, where there was an initial use case for training our own model, where it really didn't make sense to use any of the biggest foundation models. That was incredibly successful, moved to another use case that worked really well, and had been going from there. And one of the helpful things in doing this sort of model development is picking your spots carefully, not trying to reinvent the wheel, not trying to focus on places, and maybe where the best foundation models are excellent, but instead kind of focusing on their weaknesses, and how you can complement them.
turns.zh: 我认为有一点对我们来说出乎意料，[00:32:14语音中断]之前我也提到过，但确实，我们一开始根本没料到自己会进行模型开发。正如之前所说，当我们刚接触这个领域时，很多公司从一开始就专注于从零训练模型。我们之前计算过训练模型的成本，知道自己根本无法承担这项任务。而且我们觉得把精力放在错误的方向上有些得不偿失，因为市面上已经有很多优秀的模型，何必重复造轮子。特别是在预训练方面，拿一个一无所知的神经网络，然后教它整个互联网的知识。（00:32:55）所以我们原本以为自己根本不会做这些事情，从一开始我们就清楚，现有的模型有很多功能本可以为我们所用，但因为缺乏合适的工具支持而未能实现。然而事实上，我们现在做了很多模型开发工作，内部招聘时也非常重视这方面，并组建了一支出色的团队。（00:33:18）这在产品质量方面也带来了巨大提升。目前，Cursor 上的每个神奇时刻都离不开某种定制模型。所以这确实出乎意料，也令人惊喜。整个过程是循序渐进的：最初有个用例需要自定义模型，而使用主流基础模型根本不现实，结果大获成功；接着又在另一个用例上取得了出色成果。进行模型开发时，关键在于精准选点，不必重复造轮子，不必在那些优秀基础模型已能胜任的领域纠结，而是要专注于它们的短板，并找到与之互补的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is going to be surprising to a lot of people hearing that you have your own models. When people talk about Cursor and all the folks in the space, they would kind of call them GPT wrappers, they're just sitting on top of ChatGPT or Sonnet. What you're saying is that you have your own models, talk about just the stack behind the scenes.
turns.zh: 我觉得听说你们有自己的模型，很多人会感到惊讶。当人们谈论 Cursor 以及这个领域的其他公司时，通常会称他们为 GPT 封装器，就是在 ChatGPT 或 Sonnet 之上搭建应用。你们却说自己有自己的模型，能否详细讲讲背后的技术栈？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah, of course. So we definitely use the biggest foundation models a bunch of different ways, they're really important components of bringing the Cursor experience to people. The places where we use our own models, so sometimes it's to survey a use case that a foundation model wouldn't be able to serve at all for cost or speed reasons. And so one example of that is the autocomplete side of things. And so this can be a little bit tricky for people who don't code to understand, but code is this weird form of work, where sometimes, really, the next 5, 10, 20, 30 minutes of your work is entirely predictable from looking over your shoulder. (00:35:02): And I would contrast this with writing. So writing, lots of people are familiar with Gmail's autocomplete, and the different forms of autocomplete that show up when you're trying to post text messages, or emails, or things like that. They can only be so helpful, because often, it's just really not clear what you're going to be writing just by looking at what you've written before. But in code sometimes, when you edit a part of a code base, you're going to need to change things, and in other parts of code base, and it's entirely clear how you're going to need to change things. (00:35:30): So one core part of Cursor is this really suit to autocomplete experience, where you predict the next set of that you're going to be doing across multiple files, across multiple places within a file. And making models good at that use case, one, there's a speed component of, those models need to be really fast, they need to give you a completion within 300 milliseconds. There's also this cost component of, we're running tons, and tons, and tons of molecules, every keystroke, we need to be changing our prediction for what you're going to do next. And then it's also this really specialty use case of, you need models that are really good, not at completing the next token, just a generic tech sequence, but are really good at autocompleting a series of diffs, looking at what's changed within a code base, and then creating the next set of things that are going to change, both deleted and added and all of that, and we found a ton of success in training models specifically for that task. (00:36:23): So that's a place where no foundation models are involved, it's kind of our own thing. We don't have a lot of labeling or branding about this in the app, power is a very core part of Cursor. And then another set of places where a user own models are to help things like Sonnet, or Gemini, or GPT, and those sit both on the inputs of those big models, and on the output. On the input side of things, those models are searching throughout a code base, try to figure out the parts of a code base to show to one of these big models. You can kind of think about this as a mini Google search that's specifically built for finding the relevant parts of the code base to show one of these big models. (00:37:02): And then on the output side of things, we take the sketches of the changes that these models are suggesting, you make with that code base. And then we have models that then fill in the details of, the high level thinking is done by the smartest models, they spend a few tokens on doing that, and then these smaller specialty incredibly fast models, coupled with some inference tricks, then take those high level changes and turn them actually into full code diffs. And so it's been super helpful for pushing on quality in places where you need a specialty task, and it's been super helpful for pushing on speed, which is such an important dimension of product quality for us too.
turns.zh:
是的，当然。我们肯定会以多种方式使用最大的基础模型，它们是为用户带来Cursor体验的重要组成部分。在某些场景下，我们会使用自己的模型，比如当基础模型因成本或速度原因无法满足需求时，比如自动完成功能。这对不熟悉编程的人来说可能有点难理解，但编程工作很奇特，有时你接下来5分钟、10分钟、20分钟、30分钟的工作内容，光看代码就能预见个大概。（00:35:02）这和写作形成鲜明对比。很多人熟悉Gmail的自动完成功能，以及在发送短信、邮件等场景下出现的自动完成提示。但这些功能的帮助往往有限，因为仅凭之前的输入内容很难准确预测用户的下一步操作。而在编程中，当你编辑代码库的某个部分时，需要对其他代码段进行更改，而这些更改的逻辑往往清晰明了。（00:35:30）Cursor的核心功能是多文件、多位置的自动完成体验，能预测用户在多个文件、多个代码位置的下一步操作。要让模型在这种场景下表现出色，首先速度至关重要——模型必须在300毫秒内给出补全建议。成本方面，我们每一次按键操作都会触发大量模型计算，需要实时调整预测结果。此外，这类场景对模型有特殊要求：不仅要准确补全单个代码片段，还要能处理一系列差异补丁，识别代码库的变更内容，并生成下一步的变更建议（包括删除和新增代码）。我们通过专门训练的模型在这些任务上取得了显著成效。（00:36:23）这部分场景不涉及基础模型，完全是我们的独家技术。我们在应用中并未大张旗鼓地宣传这一核心功能。权力是Cursor的核心组成部分。还有一系列场景中，用户自有模型会辅助Sonnnet、Gemini或GPT等模型。这些模型既参与输入端处理，也参与输出端生成。输入端方面，模型会全局搜索代码库，筛选出适合展示给大型模型的片段。这可以视为专为查找代码库相关内容而设计的迷你谷歌搜索。输出端方面，用户根据模型建议的变更草案进行代码编辑。随后，小型专用模型通过高速推理，将这些高层级变更转化为完整的代码差异。这为提升特定场景的质量和速度带来了巨大助力。
产品质量对我们来说也是一个至关重要的方面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so interesting. I just had Kevin Weil on the podcast, CPO of OpenAI, and he calls this the ensemble of models, that's the same way-
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。我刚在播客上采访了OpenAI的首席产品官凯文·韦尔，他把这称为模型集成，这和你的观点如出一辙——

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... they work, to use the best feature of each one, and to your point, the cost advantages of using cheaper models. These other models, are they based on Llama and things like that, just open source models that you guys plug into and build on?
turns.zh: ……它们通过整合各模型的最佳特性来实现协同效应。说到成本优势，使用更廉价的模型也是一个思路吧？这些其他模型，是基于Llama之类的开源模型吗？还是说你们只是接入并在此基础上进行开发？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah. So again, we try to be very pragmatic about the place that we're going to do this work, and we don't want to reinvent the wheel. And so starting from the very best pre-trained models that exist out there, often open source ones, sometimes in collaboration with these big model providers that don't share their weights out into the world, because the thing we care about last is the ability to read line by line, the matrix of weights that then go to give you a certain output. We just care about the ability to train these things, to post-train them. And so by and large, yes, open source models, sometimes working with the closed source providers too to tune things.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们在选择技术路线时非常务实，不想重复造轮子。我们会从现有的顶级预训练模型入手，很多都是开源的，有时也会与不公开权重的巨头模型提供商合作。毕竟我们最关注的是能否逐行解读权重矩阵，最终输出符合预期。重点在于模型的可训练性和微调能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This leads to a discussion that a lot of AI founders always think about and investors, which is moats, and defensibility in AI. So it feels like one is custom models, is a moat in the space. How do you just think about long-term defensibility in the space, knowing there's other folks, as you said, launching constantly trying to eat your lunch?
turns.zh: 这引发了一个许多AI创始人和投资者都在思考的议题——护城河和AI领域的防御壁垒。自定义模型似乎是AI领域的一道护城河，但长远看，当其他公司不断涌现时，你该如何维护自己的竞争优势？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think that there are ways to build in inertia and traditional moats, but I think by and large, we're in a space where it is incumbent on us to continue to try to build the best thing, and everyone in this industry. And I truly just think that the ceiling is so high that no matter what entrenchment you build, you can be leapfrogged. And I think that this resembles markets that are maybe a little bit different from normal software markets, normal enterprise markets of the past. I think one that comes to mind is the market for search engines at the end of 1999, or at the end of the '90s and beginning of the 2000s. I think another market that comes to mind that resembles this market in many ways, it's actually just the development of the peripheral computer and many computers in the '70s, '80s, '90s. (00:40:03): And I think that, yes, in each of those markets, the ceiling was incredibly high, it was possible to swish. You could keep getting value for the incremental hour of a smart person's time, the incremental R&D dollar for a really long time, you wouldn't run out of useful things to build. And then in search in particular, not on the computer case, adding distribution was helpful for making the product better too, in that you could tune the algorithms, you could tune the learning based off of the data and the feedback you're getting from users. And I think that all of those dynamics exist in our market too. And so I think maybe the sad truth for people like us, but then the amazing truth for the world is, I think that there are many leapfrogs that exist, there's more useful things to build. We're a long way away from where we can compete in 5, 10 years, and it's incumbent in our state to keep that going.
turns.zh: 我认为传统的护城河和惯性优势确实存在，但从大局来看，这个领域要求我们持续创新，整个行业都在朝着这个方向努力。天花板太高了，无论你建立多么坚固的壁垒，都可能被超越。这与传统软件市场或企业市场不同。比如1999年末至2000年初的搜索引擎市场，以及70、80、90年代的个人电脑市场。这些市场都有极高的天花板，聪明人的增量时间和研发投入都能创造巨大价值，创新永无止境。回到搜索引擎，分发策略对优化算法和用户反馈也很重要。我们的市场也存在类似的动态。对我来说，现实是残酷的，但对世界来说却充满希望——未来还会有更多颠覆者出现，创新空间巨大。我们距离真正竞争力还很遥远，未来五年、十年都需要持续创新。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing, this sounds like a lot more like a consumer sort of moat, where it's just, be the best thing consistently so that people stick with you versus creating lock-in and things like that, where they're just... Like Salesforce, where it's just contracts with the entire company, and you have to use this product.
turns.zh: 听起来这更像是一种消费者层面的护城河策略——持续提供卓越的产品体验，让用户愿意持续使用，而不是通过锁定用户等手段来强制用户依赖。以Salesforce为例，用户只能与整个公司签订合同，必须使用该公司的产品。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah. I think the important thing to note is, if you're in a space where you run out of useful things to do very quickly, then that's not a great situation to be in. But if you're in a place where big investments, and having more and more great people working on the right path can keep giving you value, then you can get these economies of scale of R&D, and you can deeply work on the technology in the right direction, and get to a place where that is defensible. But yes, it is... I think there's a consumer-like tendency to it, and I really think it's just about building the best thing possible.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为关键在于，如果你所处的领域很快就会耗尽可开发的创新点，那么这种局面就很不利。但如果你的领域能通过大规模投资、汇聚更多优秀人才并沿着正确方向持续创新，从而不断创造价值，那么你就能获得研发的规模效益，深入研发核心技术，最终形成难以被替代的护城河。不过确实，这其中存在消费者导向的倾向，我认为关键在于打造尽可能出色的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you think in the future there's one winner in this space, or do you think it's going to be a world of a number of products like this?
turns.zh: 你认为未来这个领域会出现一家霸主，还是会形成多个产品的共存局面？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think the market is just so very big. You asked about the IDE thing early on, and one thing that I think a trip of some people that were thinking about the space is, they looked at the IDE market of the past 10 years, and they said, "Who's making money off of the editors?" It's this super fragmented space where everyone kind of has their own thing, with their own figuration, and there's one company that actually makes money off making great editors, but that company is only so big. And then the conclusion was, it was going to look like that in the future. And I think that the thing that people missed was that there was only so much you could do building an editor in the 2010s for coders, and the company that made money off of editors was doing things like making it easy to navigate around a code base, and doing some error checking and type checking for things, and having good debugging tools. (00:42:57): Which were all very useful, but I think that the set of things you can build for programmers, I think the set of things you can build for knowledge workers in many different areas just goes very far and very deep. The problem in front of all of us is the automation of a lot of busy work and knowledge work, and really changing all the areas of knowledge work in front of us to be much higher level and more productive. (00:43:19): So that was a long-winded way to say, I think the market's really, really big that we're in. I think it's much bigger than people have realized than the other building tools for developers in the past. And I think that there will be a bunch of different solutions. I think that there will be one company, to be determined if it's going to be us, but I do think that there will be one company that builds the general tool that builds almost all the world's software, and that will be a very, very generationally big business. But I think that there will be kind of niches you can occupy in doing something for a particular segment of the market, or for a very particular part of the software development life cycle. But the general programming shifts from just writing formal programming languages to something way higher level. This is the application you purchase and use to do that. I think that there will be generally one winner there, and it will be a very big business.
turns.zh: 我认为这个市场规模非常庞大。早些时候你提到的IDE工具问题，让一些思考这个领域的人意识到，过去10年IDEditor市场的情况是，谁从编辑工具中赚钱？这个市场极其分散，每个厂商都有自己的特色产品，而只有一家公司通过打造优质编辑器实现了盈利，但这家公司的规模也仅此而已。结论是，未来情况很可能还是如此。我认为人们忽略了一个关键点：2010年代为程序员打造编辑器的空间是有限的，而真正从编辑器中获利的公司，主要提供的功能包括代码库导航、错误检查、类型检查和调试工具等，这些都非常实用。但我认为，为知识型员工服务的工具范围，远比我们想象的要广阔得多。摆在我们面前的挑战是如何自动化大量繁琐的重复工作和知识型工作，真正将我们所面临的知识型工作领域提升到更高水平、更具生产力的境界。（00:42:57）这话说得有点长，但我想说明的是，我们所处的市场规模非常巨大，远超过去人们对开发者工具市场的认知。我认为会有多种解决方案出现，也许会有一家公司胜出——当然不确定是否会是我们——但肯定会有一家公司打造出能支撑全球软件开发的通用工具，这将是一项具有划时代意义的业务。不过也会有细分领域，比如针对特定市场或软件开发生命周期某个环节的解决方案。但编程领域正在从编写正式编程语言转向更高层次的应用。这正是你购买和使用的应用程序所能实现的。我相信这个领域最终会有一家巨头诞生，而且这将是一项极具价值的业务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Juicy. Along those lines, it's interesting that Microsoft was actually at the center of this first, with an amazing product, amazing distribution, Copilot you said was the thing that got you over the hump of, "Wow, there could be something really big here." And it doesn't feel like they're winning, it feels like they're falling behind. What do you think happened there?
turns.zh: 真有意思。顺着这个思路，有趣的是，微软实际上是这场革命的核心，他们推出了令人惊叹的产品和出色的分发策略。Copilot这款产品曾让你惊呼“哇，这里可能会有大动作！”但现在看来，微软似乎并没有占据上风，反而显得落后了。你认为这其中的原因是什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think that there are specific historical reasons why Copilot might not have lived up... So far have lived up to the expectations that some people have for it, and then I think that there are structural reasons. I think the structural reason is... And to be clear, Microsoft, in the Copilot case, obviously a big inspiration for our work, and in general, I think they do lots of awesome things, and we're users of many Microsoft products, but I think that this is a market that's not super friendly to incumbents, in that a market that's friendly to incumbents might be one where there's only so much to do, it kind of gets commoditized fairly quickly, and you can bundle that in with other products, and where the ROI between different products is quite small. And in that case, perhaps it doesn't make sense to buy the innovative solution, it makes sense to just kind of buy the thing that's bundled in with other stuff. (00:45:31): Another market that might be particularly helpful for incumbents is one where there's... From the get-go, you have your stuff in one place, and it's really, really excruciatingly hard to switch, and for better or for worse. I think in our case, you can try out different tools, and you can decide which product you think is better. And so that's not super friendly to incumbents, and that's more friendly to whoever you think is going to have the most innovative product. And then the specific historical reasons, as I understand them are the group of people that worked on the first version of Copilot have, by and large, gone on to do other things at other places. I think it's been a little hard to coordinate among all the different departments and parties that might be involved in making something like this.
turns.zh: 我认为Copilot未能达到预期有特定的历史原因……到目前为止，Copilot未能达到某些人的预期。另外，我认为还有结构性原因。结构性原因在于……需要明确的是，在Copilot案例中，微软显然是我们工作的重大灵感来源，总体而言，我认为他们做了很多出色的事情，我们也是许多微软产品的用户，但我认为这个市场对现有巨头并不友好。友好的市场可能只有有限的发展空间，很快就会被商品化，还能与其他产品捆绑销售，不同产品之间的投资回报率也很低。在这种情况下，购买创新解决方案可能没有意义，购买与其他产品捆绑的服务反而更划算。（00:45:31）对现有巨头特别有利的另一个市场是，一开始就将产品集成到现有生态中，用户切换成本极高，无论好坏都深陷其中。就我们而言，用户可以试用不同工具，选择更优的产品。这对现有巨头不利，却对最具创新力的公司有利。至于具体的历史原因，据我了解，Copilot第一版的开发团队大多已转投其他公司。协调不同部门和参与方开发此类产品确实存在挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to Cursor. A question I like to ask everyone that's building a tool like this, if you could sit next to every new user that uses Cursor for the first time, just whisper a couple tips in their ear to be more successful, most successful with Cursor, what would be 1 or 2 tips?
turns.zh: 回到Cursor。我想问每个开发类似工具的人，如果你能坐在每位首次使用Cursor的新用户身边，在他们耳边低语两个成功秘诀，你会说什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think right now, and we'd want to fix this at a product level, a lot of being successful with Cursor is kind of having a taste for what the models can do, both what complexity of a task they can handle, and how much you need to specify things to that model, but having a taste for the quality of the model, and where its gaps exist, and what it can do and what it can't. And right now, we don't do a good job in the product of educating people around that, and maybe giving people some swim lanes, giving people some guidelines. (00:47:06): But to develop that taste, would give two tips. So one is, as mentioned before, would bias less toward, trying in one go to tell the model, "Hey, here's exactly what I want you to do." Then seeing the output, and then either being disappointed or accepting the entire thing for an entire big task. Instead what I would do is I would chop things up into bits, and you can spend basically the same amount of time specifying things overall, but chopped up more. So you're specifying a little bit, you're getting a little bit of work, you're specifying a little bit, getting a little bit of work, and not doing as much the, "Let's write a giant thing telling the model exactly what to do." I think that will be a little bit of a recipe for disaster right now. (00:47:48): And so biasing toward chopping things up. At the same time, and it might make sense to do this on a side project and not on your professional work, I would encourage people to, especially developers who are used to existing workflows for building software, I would encourage people to explicitly try to fall on their face, and try to discover the limits of what these models can do by being ambitious in a safe environment, like perhaps a side project, and trying to kind of go around town, use AI to the fullest. Because a lot of the time, we run into people who haven't given the AI yet a fair shake, and are underestimating its abilities. So generally biasing towards chopping things up and making things smaller, but to discover the limits of what you can do there, explicitly just try to go for broke in a safe environment, and get a taste for... You might be surprised in some of the places where the model doesn't break.
turns.zh: 我认为当下，在产品层面，我们需要解决这个问题。要想在Cursor上取得成功，关键在于要了解模型能处理的任务复杂度，以及需要向模型提供多少指导信息，同时还要评估模型的质量，识别其存在的局限性，以及能做什么、不能做什么。目前，我们的产品在向用户传授这些知识方面做得不够，也许可以为用户提供一些指导方针。（00:47:06）：但要培养这种洞察力，我有两个建议。首先，正如之前提到的，要减少对模型的过度指导，比如一开始就试图告诉模型“你必须准确完成我的任务”。然后看到输出结果后，要么感到失望，要么接受整个任务。而我建议把任务拆分成小块。虽然总的来说需要花费同样多的时间进行指导，但拆分后的任务更易于管理。你可以先给出一点指示，完成一部分工作，再给出一点指示，完成另一部分工作。而不是一股脑地写一大段代码告诉模型该怎么做。我认为现在这样做很可能适得其反。（00:47:48）：所以要倾向于拆分任务。同时，对于副业项目而非专业工作，这或许更可行。我鼓励大家，尤其是习惯现有软件开发流程的开发者，主动在安全的环境中（比如副业项目）大胆尝试，充分利用AI的能力。这能帮助我们发现模型的局限性，因为很多时候人们低估了AI的能力。因此，关键在于拆分任务、降低复杂度，在安全的环境中全力以赴探索模型的极限。你可能会惊讶地发现模型在某些场景下无法处理的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm essentially hearing is build a gut feeling of what the model can do, and how far it can take an idea versus just kind of guiding it along. And I bet that you need to rebuild this gut every time there's a new model launch, when it's on... I don't know, 4.0 comes out, you have to do this again. Is that generally right?
turns.zh: 我理解的核心是，要建立对模型能力的直觉理解，知道它能在多大程度上实现你的构想，而不只是被动地引导它。我敢打赌，每次有新模型发布时，比如4.0版本上线，你都需要重新建立这种直觉。这对吗？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yes. For the past few years, it hasn't been as big as I think the first experience people have had with some of these big models. This is also a problem we would hope to solve much better just for users, and take the burden off of them. But each of these things have slightly different quirks and different personalities.
turns.zh: 是的。过去几年里，新模型给人们带来的惊喜远不如最初体验那么强烈。这也是我们希望能更好地为用户解决的问题，减轻他们的负担。但每个模型都有细微的特性和不同的个性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, something that people are always debating tools like Cursor, are they more helpful to junior engineers, or are they more helpful to senior engineers? Do they make senior engineers 10X better? Do they make junior engineers more like senior engineers? Who do you think benefits most today from Cursor?
turns.zh: 关于这点，人们总在讨论像Cursor这样的工具，它对初级工程师更有帮助，还是对高级工程师更有帮助？它们能让高级工程师的效率提升10倍吗？能让初级工程师更接近高级工程师的水平吗？你认为如今谁能从Cursor中获益最多？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think across the board. Both of these cohorts benefit in big ways. It's a little hard to say on the relative ranking. I will say, they fall into different anti-patterns. The junior engineers we see going a little too wholesale, relying on AI for everything, and we're not yet in a place where you can kind of do that end-to-end on a professional tool, working with tens, hundreds of other people within a long-lived code base. And then the senior engineers... For many folks, it's not true for all, and we actually often... One of the ways these tools are adopted is, there's developer experience teams within companies, often those are staffed by incredibly senior people, because often, those are people who are building tools to make the rest of the engineers within an organization more productive. (00:50:33): And we've seen some very, very boundary pushing kind of... We've seen people who are on the front lines of really trying to adopt the technology as much as possible there. But by and large, I would say on average, as a group, the senior engineers underrate what AI can do for them, and stick to their existing workflows. And so the relative ranking is a little hard, I think they fall into different anti-patterns, but they both, by and large, yet get big benefits with these tools.
turns.zh: 我认为总体而言，这两类工程师都能从中获益良多。但要说具体的相对排名就有点难了。不过我可以说，他们各自陷入了不同的反模式。初级工程师往往有些急功近利，凡事都依赖AI，但目前我们还未能在专业工具中实现端到端的全流程应用——毕竟在一个长期维护的代码库中，与数十、数百名其他工程师协作时，这种做法往往行不通。而资深工程师方面……虽然并非所有人都如此，但我们确实经常观察到这样一个现象：这些工具的采用过程中，公司内部通常会组建开发者体验团队，成员多由资深人士组成，因为这些团队往往负责开发工具，以提升组织内其他工程师的生产力。（00:50:33）：我们见过一些非常激进的……比如那些奋不顾身、尽可能全面应用新技术的前线人员。但总体而言，我认为资深工程师群体普遍低估了AI能为他们带来的价值，依然固守现有工作流程。因此，要对他们的相对排名进行评判确实不易。虽然他们各自陷入了不同的反模式，但总体而言，这两类工程师都能从这些工具中获得显著收益。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes absolute sense. I love that it's two ends of the spectrum, expect too much, don't expect enough. It's like the three bears allegory.
turns.zh: 这说得太有道理了。我喜欢这种两极分化的现象——要么期望过高，要么期望不足。这就像《三只熊》的寓言故事。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Okay.
turns.zh: 对。好的。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe the sort of senior, but not staff, right in the middle.
turns.zh: 是啊。或许是那种资深但非管理层的角色，处于两者之间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Okay. Just a couple more questions. What's something that you wish you knew before you got into this role? If you could go back to Michael at the beginning of Cursor, which was not that long ago, and you could give him some advice, what's something that you would tell him?
turns.zh: 有意思。好的。再问几个问题。你希望在入职这个岗位前就了解哪些知识？如果你能回到不久前《Cursor》项目刚开始时的迈克尔，给他一些建议，你会说什么？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: The tough thing with this is, it feels like so much of the hard-won knowledge is tacit, and a bit hard to communicate verbally. And the sad fact of life feels like for some areas of human endeavor, you kind of do need to fall on your face to... Either need to fall on your face to learn the correct thing, or you need to be around someone who's a great example of excellence in the thing. And one area where we have felt this is hiring. I think that we actually were... So we tried to be incredibly patient on the hiring front. (00:52:20): It was really important to us that, both for personal reasons and also for, I think actually for the company's strategy, having a world-class group of engineers and researchers to work on Cursor with us was going to be incredibly important. Also, getting people who fit... A certain mix of intellectual curiosity and experimentation, because there can be so many new things we need to build. And then also an intellectual honesty, and maybe micro-pessimism, bluntness, because if all the noise, and... Especially as the company's grown, and the business has grown, keeping a level head I think is incredibly important too. (00:52:59): But getting the right group of people into the company was the thing that maybe more than anything else, apart from building the product, we really, really fussed over. We actually waited a long time to grow the team because of that. And I think that many people you hear hired too fast, think we actually hired too slow to begin with. I think it could have been remedied, I think we could have been better at it. (00:53:28): And the method of recruiting that we ended up eventually falling into and working really well for us, which isn't that novel, of going after people that we think are really world-class, and recruiting them over the course of, in some cases, many years, ended up working for us in the end, but I don't think we were very good at it to begin with. And so I think that there were hard-won lessons around both who was the right profile, who actually made sense in that team, what did greatness look like, and then how to talk with someone about the opportunity, and get them excited if they really weren't looking for anything. There were lots of learnings there about how to do that well, and that took us a bit of time.
turns.zh:
难点在于，许多来之不易的知识似乎都隐藏在不言自明的层面，很难用语言清晰传达。令人遗憾的是，在某些人类活动领域，你确实需要亲身经历挫折才能领悟真谛——要么在错误中吸取教训，要么身边必须有卓越典范的榜样。招聘就是我们深有体会的领域之一。出于个人原因和公司战略考量，组建一支世界级的工程师与研究团队与我们共同打造Cursor项目至关重要。同时，我们还需要吸引那些兼具求知欲、实验精神、开放心态和微观悲观主义的人才——毕竟新技术的研发会带来诸多挑战。保持理性思维和直言不讳的品质也至关重要，因为在公司规模扩大、业务复杂化后，冷静判断尤为关键。

（00:52:20）但在招聘人才这件事上，我们的投入远超产品开发本身。正因如此，我们曾长时间暂缓扩充团队规模。如今许多人批评我们招聘速度过慢，我认为这种担忧不无道理。我们本可以做得更好，比如更早发现并吸引顶尖人才。

（00:53:28）最终我们采用了一种成熟的招聘策略：锁定世界级人才，分阶段、历时数年完成招募。这种方法虽不算创新，但最终效果显著。不过最初我们做得很不到位。在识别合适人选、评估其团队适应性、定义卓越标准，以及如何有效传递机遇价值方面，我们都积累了深刻教训。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some of those learnings for folks that are hiring right now? What's something you missed or learned?
turns.zh: 对于当前正在招聘的人来说，哪些经验值得借鉴？你们是否有遗漏或总结的要点？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think to start with, maybe we actually biased a little bit too much towards looking for people who fit the archetype of well-known school, very young, had done the things that were high credential in those well-known school environments. And actually, I think found... Were lucky early on to find fantastic people who are willing to do this with us who were later careered. I think we should kind of spent a bunch of time on maybe a little bit the wrong profile to begin with, and part of that was a seniority thing. Part of that was kind of an interest and experience thing too, we have hired people who are excellent, excellent, excellent and very young, but they maybe look in some cases slightly different from being straight out of central casting. (00:55:12): Another lesson is just, we very much evolved our interview loop, and so now, we have a hand-rolled set of interview questions, and then core our... Core to how we interview too, is actually, we have people onsite for two days, and do a project with us, a work test project. And that has worked really well, that increasingly you're finding that. I think how to learn about what people are interested in, and put our best foot forward, and letting them know about the opportunity when they're really not looking for anything, and have those conversations. There's definitely been... Gotten better at that over time.
turns.zh: 我认为首先，我们可能在寻找人才时过于偏向于那些出身名校、年轻且在知名学府环境中表现出色的人才。实际上，我认为我们曾幸运地早期招到了愿意与我们共事的优秀人才，而这些人才后来也成长为行业领袖。我认为我们或许一开始就花了大量时间在错误的候选人画像上，部分原因在于资历偏好，部分原因在于兴趣和经验匹配。我们确实招聘了极其优秀、极其年轻的人才，但他们有时看起来与传统招聘标准略有不同。（00:55:12）：另一个经验是，我们对面试流程进行了重大改进。现在，我们制定了一套手动设计的面试问题，并将核心面试环节延长至两天，让候选人参与实际项目测试。这种方式效果显著，越来越多的候选人因此获得了深刻印象。我认为关键在于如何了解他们的兴趣点、展现我们的优势、在他们尚未主动寻找机会时向他们传递机遇，并开展深度沟通。随着时间推移，我们在这方面确实有所提升。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite interview question that you like to ask?
turns.zh: 你有没有特别喜欢的面试问题？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think this two-day work test which we thought would not scale past a few people has had surprising staying power. And the great thing about it is, it lets someone go end-to-end on it like a real project. It's not work that we use, it's canned list of projects. But it gives you two days of seeing a real work product, and it doesn't have to be incredibly time-enhancing other teams from time. You can take the time you would spend in a half day or one day onsite, and you kind of spread it out over those two days, and give someone a lot of time to do work on their projects, and so that can actually help it scale. (00:56:38): It helps to enforce, do you want to be around this person type test, because you are around this person for two days, a bunch of meals with them. We didn't expect that one to stick around, but that has been really, really important to our value to process, and then also important to getting people excited at, especially the very early stages of the company. Because before, people are using the product, and know about it. And when the product is comparatively not very good, really, the only thing you have going for you is a team of people that some people find special and want to be around. And the two days would give us a chance to just have this person meet us, and in some cases, hopefully get convinced that they want to throw in with us. That one was unexpected. Not exactly an interview question, but kind of like a forward interview.
turns.zh: 我认为这个为期两天的项目测试超出了我们最初的预期。它的优势在于让候选人能像参与真实项目一样全程沉浸其中。我们并非采用现成的项目列表，而是量身定制的测试内容。这让他们有两天时间产出真实成果，同时无需占用其他团队的宝贵时间。你可以将原本半天或一天的现场时间分摊到两天，让候选人有充足时间专注项目开发，这实际上有助于规模化实施。（00:56:38）：这种方式能强化评估标准，因为候选人需要与我们共度两天时光，共进多餐。我们原本没料到这种深度接触会如此重要，但它对我们的招聘流程和初期团队凝聚力至关重要。在早期阶段，用户尚未广泛使用产品，产品体验也相对欠佳，此时团队的独特魅力成为唯一的竞争优势。两天的相处时间能让候选人深入了解我们，并有机会被说服加入团队。这次改进确实出乎意料。虽然这不算严格意义上的面试问题，但更像是一种前置面试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The ultimate interview question. So just to be very clear about what you're describing, you give them an assignment, like, "Build this feature in our actual code base, work with the team to code it and ship it." Is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 终极面试问题。那么，我是否理解得正确——你会给他们布置任务，比如“在我们的实际代码库中开发这个功能，与团队合作完成并上线”？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yes. So we don't use the IP, not shift end-to-end, but it's like a mock... Very often in our code base, "Here's a real mini two-day project. You're going to do it end-to-end." Largely being left alone, there's collaboration too. And then we're a pretty imprisoned company, in almost all cases, it's actually just sitting in office with us too.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们不使用IP，也不进行端到端的转换，但这就像是一个模拟……在我们的代码库中，经常会出现这样的情况：“这里有一个真正的两天迷你项目。你要从头到尾完成它。” 大部分情况下大家各自忙碌，也有协作的时候。然后我们是一家相当受限的公司，几乎所有情况下，大家都只是坐在办公室里工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you've been saying that this has scaled to even today, so how big are you guys at this point?
turns.zh: 你之前说过这种模式一直延续到现在，那你们现在规模有多大了？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: So we are going on 60 people.
turns.zh: 我们现在有60多人了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So small for the scale and impact. I was thinking it'd be a lot larger than that.
turns.zh: 就规模和影响力而言规模还是太小了。我原以为会大得多。

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I imagine the largest percent is engineers?
turns.zh: 我猜工程师占的比例最大吧？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: Yeah. To be clear, a big part of the work ahead of us is building a group of people that is bigger, and awesome, and can continue to make the product better, and the service we give to customers better. And so you don't plan to stay that small for longer, wouldn't hope so. But part of the reason that that number is small is, the percentage of engineering and research and design is very high within the company, and so many software companies when they have roughly 40 engineers would be over 100 people, because there's lots of operational work, and often, they're very, very sales-led from the get-go, and that's just quite labor-intensive. And here, we started from a place of being incredibly lean in product-led, and we now serve lots of our market customers, and it built that out, but there's much more to do there.
turns.zh: 是的。说实话，我们面临的首要任务是组建一支更庞大、更优秀的团队，让他们能够持续提升产品质量，优化为客户提供的服务。所以你们不打算一直保持这么小的规模，对吧？但团队规模较小的原因之一是，公司内部工程、研发和设计的比例非常高，而许多软件公司当有40名工程师时，员工规模可能超过100人，因为有很多运营工作，而且往往从一开始就以销售为导向，这非常耗费人力。而我们从一开始就以极度精简的产品为导向，现在已经为许多市场客户提供服务，但还有很多工作要做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A question I wanted to ask you, there's so much happening in AI, there's things launching every... There's newsletters, many newsletters, whose entire function is to tell you what is happening in AI every single day. Running a company that's at the center, the white-hot center of this space, how do you stay focused, and how do you help your team stay focused, and heads down, and just build and not get distracted by all these shiny things?
turns.zh: 我想问你一个问题，现在AI领域有很多动态，每天都有新产品发布……有许多新闻通讯专门报道AI领域的每日动态。作为一家处于这个领域核心位置的公司，你们是如何保持专注的，又如何帮助团队专注于核心任务，埋头开发而不会被这些光鲜事物分心？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: I think hiring is a big part of it, and if you get people with the right attitude. All of this should be asterisked in, I think we're doing well there, I think that we'd probably be doing better there too, and it's something that we should probably talk even more about as a company. But I think that hiring people with the right disposition, people who are less focused on external validation, more focused on building something really great, more focused on doing really high quality work, and people who are just generally level-headed, and maybe the highs aren't very high, the lows aren't very low. I think hiring can get you through a lot here, and I think that's actually a learning throughout the company, is that for any... You need process, you need hierarchy, you need lots of things, but for any kind of organizational tool that you're introducing into a company, the result you're looking to get from that tool also... You can go pretty far on hiring people with the right behaviors that you want to resolve from that for organizational thing. (01:00:39): And the specific example that comes to mind is, we've been able to get away with not a ton of process yet on the engineering front, and I think we need a little bit more process, but for our size, not a ton of process, by hiring people who I think are really excellent. One is hiring people that are level-headed. I think two is just talking about it a lot. I think three is hopefully leading by example. And for us personally, we've since 2021, 2022 been professionally working on this, and been working on AI, and we've just seen a sea change of the comings and goings of various technologies and ideas of... If you're to transport yourself back to end of 2021, beginning of 2022, this is GPT-3, Instruct GPT doesn't exist, there's no Dolly, there's no stable diffusion. And then we've gone through all of those image technologies existing, ChatGPT and that rise, and GPT-4, all of these new models, all these different modalities, all the video stuff, and only a very small number of these things really kind of affects the business. (01:01:45): So I think we've kind of just built up a little bit of an immune system, and know when an event comes around that actually is really going to matter for us. This dynamic too of there being lots, and lots, and lots of chatter, but then maybe only a few things that really matter, I think has been mirrored in AI over the last decade, where there have been so many papers on deep learning in academia, so many papers on AI in academia, then the amazing thing is there are really a lot of... A lot the progress of AI can be attributed to some very simple elegant ideas that have stayed around, and the vast majority of ideas that have been put out there haven't had staying power, and haven't mattered a ton. And so the dynamic is a little bit mirrored in the evolution of deep learning as a field overall.
turns.zh:
我认为招聘是其中的关键环节，如果能招到具备正确心态的人才至关重要。我觉得这部分内容需要特别强调。我们在这方面做得不错，但或许还能做得更好，整个公司都应该对此进行更深入的探讨。关键在于招聘具备正确价值观的人才——他们不应过度追逐外界认可，而是专注于打造卓越产品，致力于高质量的工作，保持稳重的心态，既不妄自菲薄，也不妄自尊大。招聘策略能在很大程度上帮助我们克服挑战。整个公司都意识到，任何组织变革工具（比如流程、层级制度等）最终都必须服务于特定目标，而招聘恰恰能为达成这些目标提供助力。

（01:00:39）举个具体例子：在工程部门，我们暂时还不需要过多依赖严格的流程，但考虑到公司规模，适度规范化流程还是必要的。关键在于招聘具备正确价值观的人才。首先，招到头脑冷静的人才至关重要。其次，持续沟通至关重要。第三，希望能以身作则。自2021年和2022年以来，我们持续专注于AI技术，见证了诸多技术与理念的更迭：GPT-3、Instruct GPT、Dolly、Stable Diffusion等。回望2021底、2022年初，人们对ChatGPT的狂热还闻所未闻。如今，GPT-4等新模型层出不穷，视频应用蓬勃发展，但真正能对业务产生实质性影响的技术屈指可数。

（01:01:45）我们已逐渐形成免疫机制，能准确判断哪些趋势真正影响业务。AI领域过去十年的发展也呈现出类似动态：学术界充斥着深度学习与AI相关的论文，但真正经得起时间考验的核心理念却寥寥无几。深层学习领域的演进轨迹与AI整体发展颇为相似——海量理论诞生，但绝大多数未能站稳脚跟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Last question. What do you think people still most misunderstand, or maybe don't fully grasp about where things are heading with AI in building in the way the world will change?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题：您认为人们对AI如何重塑世界的认知仍存在哪些误解或未能充分理解的领域？

turns.speaker: Michael Truell
turns.en: People are still a little bit occupied too much, either end of a spectrum of it's all going to happen very fast, and this is all bluster, and hype, and snake well, and I think we're in the middle of a technology shift that's going to be incredibly consequential.
